The Challenge of Cheap Interventions and Expensive Clinical Trials https://www.fightaging.org/archives/2026/09/the-challenge-of-cheap-interventions-and-expensive-clinical-trials/

There are a good many affordable interventions that may well produce enough of an effect on aging to justify widespread use. At the more compelling end of the spectrum, based on a relatively large effect size in animal data and very limited supporting human data, we might consider the senolytic combination of dasatinib and quercetin, stem cell and exosome therapies, and fecal microbiota transplantation from a young donor to an old recipient. Somewhere in the middle lies rapamycin and some bisphosphonate therapies for osteoporosis. At the less compelling end of the list, based on an expectation of smaller positive outcomes and very mixed data for any effect on aging, we find widely used interventions such as hyperbaric oxygen therapy.

But we don't know with reasonable certainty for any of these interventions that it is in fact useful in the matter of aging, as that reasonable certainty requires at least a few fairly large clinical trials, summing to a patient population of high hundreds to low thousands at minimum. Interventions that only slow aging would also require those trials to last a long time, at least five years, in order to generate a meaning signal from incidence of age-related death and disease.

The challenge faced by all affordable interventions, capable of being readily implemented by most clinics, is that no-one has much of a motivation to fund a clinical program that would provide confidence in their ability to slow or reverse aging in specific ways. Regulators in the wealthier parts of the world, in collaboration with large pharmaceutical companies, have made the process of running a responsible clinical trial so very expensive that only a small fraction of the space of all possible therapies can possibly make enough of a profit to justify the investment. Anything that is hard to patent, and thereby obtain some degree of monopoly on the market, is not interesting to investors. Outside of the pharmaceutical and biotech industries, there is only limited funding for clinical trials from other sources, such as academia.

So we have the situation in which therapies potentially applicable to aging can exist in the market for decades without any sufficiently rigorous attempt being made to determine (a) whether they can treat aging, and (b) how good they are at treating aging. What can be done about this?

A variety of initiatives have been underway for some time, to some degree. Some groups want to reduce the cost of medical regulation. Thirty years of very aggressive lobbying, patient advocacy, and activism on this front have yielded just about nothing. Less than nothing, really, as the cost of putting a drug through the FDA regulatory system has more than doubled in recent decades, and the pace at which new drugs are approved keeps falling. It remains to be seen as to whether the present green shoots in the US regulatory system, such as Right to Try laws, will make any difference, but so far rhetoric from inside the system about accelerated approvals and reducing costs remains rhetoric.

A subset of those interested in reducing the cost of regulation are specifically engaged with the question of how to make clinical trials cost less. This is a complicated topic, and little progress has been made for many of the same reasons that regulation is expensive in the first place. Those in charge have little short term incentive to reduce the costs of the system; bureaucrats use it to diffuse blame for failures, while large pharmaceutical companies use the high cost of development as a moat to defend against upstart competitors. Everyone involves recognizes the flaws in the system, and no-one does anything about it because it is not in their immediate interest to do so.

Some groups devote themselves to making therapies available outside the major regulatory systems, via medical tourism. This has been relatively successful in the provision of therapies, albeit to a comparatively small number of people relative to those that could be reached if treatments were available in heavily regulated regions, but it has absolutely failed to generate an environment in which hard, reliable data on the efficacy of such therapies results. The medical tourism field is a black box; one roughly knows what therapies are available, but that is about it. Everything else is hidden, unavailable. First generation stem cell therapies have been widely used for more than 20 years, and we still know relatively little about efficacy in most use cases.

Some groups are trying to build systems and communities for self-experimentation and medical tourism participants that are specifically designed to yield higher quality data that might form the basis for synthetic clinical trials. So far this has not generated any meaningful success. It is a hard problem. All of the incentives are for patients and clinics not to share, and if one is paying enough to change those incentives, one is back to effectively running a less well organized form of expensive clinical trial.

Overall the problem of proving that an affordable therapy is or is not worthwhile as a treatment for degenerative aging is a challenging mess. For my part, I suspect that producing good data on low-cost interventions is going to require, at least at the outset, for the first dozen or so interventions, a community of dedicated, wealthy philanthropists who care more about this topic than they do about being wealthy. To my eyes, philanthropic support of clinical trials is the only short-term practical approach to bring change that might demolish the present set of perverse incentives, or at least lead to a few of the most interesting of the affordable potential interventions for aging being proven and quantified in clinical trials.
The Adaptive Cost Hypothesis of Aging, a Viewpoint on Antagonist Pleiotropy https://www.fightaging.org/archives/2026/09/the-adaptive-cost-hypothesis-of-aging-a-viewpoint-on-antagonist-pleiotropy/

At the high level, without delving into specific mechanisms, the consensus view on aging is that it exists in the shadow of natural selection. The selection pressure that drives the spread of changes in genes, systems, biology in general in any given species operates most strongly on early life reproductive success. This inevitably gives rise to systems that perform well initially, but which fall apart later. Expenditure of resources on long-term maintenance loses out to expenditure of resources on short-term reproductive fitness. Aging is a near universal side-effect of evolutionary competition, a race to the bottom that exists because early life reproductive success wins out over repeated reproductive success for a longer period of time.

That a given aspect of an individual's biochemistry can be beneficial in early life and harmful in later life is known as antagonistic pleiotropy. There are many examples at all scales, ranging from the structure and behavior of the adaptive immune system and its limited capacity for memory, to the well-known trade-off between developmental growth and later risk of age-related disease, to activities of specific proteins such VGLL3. There is a great deal of literature on this topic. Today's open access paper thus treads familiar ground in discussing aging as a side-effect of evolutionary pressures, attempting a modestly different framing of the situation.
Living Beyond Our Evolutionary Warranty: Why Non-Communicable Diseases May Be The Inevitable Costs of an Extended Lifespan

Despite decades of research, age-related non-communicable diseases (NCDs) remain prevalent even in populations with healthcare access. The conventional explanation invokes "evolutionary mismatch": modern lifestyles clash with ancestral biology. Yet a paradox persists: even individuals maintaining optimal health behaviours eventually develop NCDs. Hunter-gatherers living in ancestral conditions show moderate signs of atherosclerosis, metabolic dysfunction, and immune senescence past age 60-70. This raises the question, "Why are NCDs so difficult to prevent?"

We hereby propose an alternative framework where many NCDs represent not preventable consequences of modern lifestyle, but rather inevitable costs of adaptive mechanisms that were never "designed" to operate over 70 to 90-year lifespans. This "Adaptive Cost Hypothesis" (ACH) reframes NCDs as manifestations of evolutionary trade-offs largely, though not absolutely, between early-life fitness advantages and late-life pathology-trade-offs subject to sharply attenuated selection because they occur long after reproductive success. Late-life pathology is intrinsic to epigenetically programmed adaptive responses, manifesting even under matched environmental conditions. This is not mismatch. It is the inevitable cost of adaptive mechanisms operating beyond their evolved design duration.

Semaglutide to Reduce Calorie Intake Slows Aging in Female Mice, as Might be Expected https://www.fightaging.org/archives/2026/09/semaglutide-to-reduce-calorie-intake-slows-aging-in-female-mice-as-might-be-expected/

Without careful study design, studies in which the use of GLP-1 receptor agonists such as semaglutide lowered calorie intake significantly via suppression of appetite might be expected to teach us little that we did not already know. Reducing calorie intake without compromising minimum necessary levels of essential nutrients slows aging and extends life, whether achieved via limiting food availability or by limiting appetite. Researchers know this, and they know a great deal about the fine details of the metabolic response to reduced nutrient availability. The effects of reduced calorie intake readily overpowers the effects of other mechanisms that may or may not be operating as a result of GLP-1 receptor agonism, particularly in short-lived species. One has to look more carefully to see any more interesting outcomes that lie outside the normal effects of calorie restriction.

Reported in today's open access paper, researchers conducted a study in mice in which (a) GLP-1 receptor agonism reduced calorie intake by a quarter when started in late life, and (b) the mice lived ~15% longer. That falls in line with the results of many calorie restriction studies conducted in aged mice over the past twenty years. Indeed, the researchers conducted their own calorie restriction study with a reduced calorie intake matched to the results of their GLP-1 receptor agonist study, and found the outcomes in health to be very similar. There are a few differences, however. Why do those differences exist? GLP-1 receptor agonism affects some aspects of metabolism that calorie restriction does not, and vice versa. Most notably, calorie restricted mice are hungry for much of the time, while mice treated with GLP-1 receptor agonists are not. The signaling associated with the hunger response has its own effects on metabolism distinct from those resulting directly from sensing of nutrient levels in cells.
Late-life semaglutide treatment slows ageing and extends lifespan in female mice

Preclinical studies in disease mouse models and clinical studies have revealed pleiotropic beneficial effects of GLP-1R activation, including improved glucose and weight control, and reduced cardiovascular, renal, hepatic, and neurodegenerative disease burden. We found that GLP-1R activation late in life improved physiological function and extended lifespan in an ageing mouse model (20-month-old female C57BL/6) treated with a defined semaglutide regimen that reduced food intake by 24%. Female mice were selected to minimize confounding effects of male aggression and injury, consistent with previous long-term ageing studies. Within the end points monitored in the study, we did not observe adverse effects attributable to semaglutide. While GLP-1 medicines are widely used clinically, whether GLP-1R activation modulates ageing trajectories and lifespan in humans will require long-term clinical studies designed to evaluate ageing-related outcomes in older populations.

Our findings establish that GLP-1R activation late in life alleviates broadly ageing-associated decline and phenocopies the molecular and physiological benefits of calorie restriction. In aged female C57BL/6 mice, semaglutide treatment extended lifespan, improved physiological function, reduced hallmarks of ageing (such as stem cell attrition, inflammation, cellular senescence, genomic instability, mitochondrial dysfunction, and loss of proteostasis) and modulated the genetic regulators of ageing and nutrient sensors in the same manner as calorie restriction. The restoration of neural stem cells and neurogenesis in aged mice was particularly marked, considering the emerging evidence that GLP-1 medicines have beneficial effects on neurodegeneration.

Direct comparison of semaglutide treatment with matched calorie restriction further showed a set of comparable effects across several aspects of ageing-associated physiological decline, consistent with the idea that GLP-1 medicines can act as calorie restriction mimetics. As ageing is the biggest risk factor for numerous chronic diseases and calorie restriction slows ageing and ameliorates a broad spectrum of ageing-associated diseases, our findings raise the possibility that GLP-1 medicines may influence a wide array of seemingly unrelated diseases by slowing ageing.

Suggesting the Longevity Community Follow the Cardiovascular Community's Model for Public Messaging https://www.fightaging.org/archives/2026/09/suggesting-the-longevity-community-follow-the-cardiovascular-communitys-model-for-public-messaging/

Every field of specialist knowledge consists of a series of concentric circles, the greatest knowledge at the center, the scientists advancing the state of the art, and the least knowledge at the outskirts, the public at large. In between we find lesser scientists, patient advocates, laypeople with a strong interest in the field, and so forth - various gradations of knowledge. The members of any given ring engage in an educational dialog with the next ring out, and themselves learn from the education efforts of the more knowledgeable neighboring inner ring. The more distant any two rings are, the less they tend to engage with one another directly.

Thus we end up with the edifice of public messaging, simplifications of scientific knowledge intended for people who will never spend much time delving into a field, and largely constructed by those who are not the most knowledgeable specialists in the field. Some of these simplifications are better than others, depending on the incentives of those creating them. It seems a necessary evil, given the way the world works. We all have the freedom to pursue a greater understanding in the aspects of life and technology that we consider important, but far from enough time to become a polymath. Some shortcuts are necessary in the service of doing some good in the world.
An aging essential 8: closing the gap between geroscience and the public it serves

Longevity medicine has reached an uncomfortable milestone: more clinically credible than at any prior point, and simultaneously more publicly confused. Senolytics, partial epigenetic reprogramming, and GLP-1 metabolic agents have entered human trials within a single decade. Alongside that progress, biological age tests, longevity clinics, and consumer wearables have scaled well ahead of any shared standard governing what they measure or what a person should do with the result. The field has begun to describe this as an implementation gap, in which biological age products and clinics operate ahead of validated standards and regulatory frameworks. The remedies under active discussion are directed at research and clinical infrastructure: standardizing what longevity clinics measure, how they are structured, and which biomarkers and outcomes should count. Few of them address the layer that ordinary people actually encounter, which is a number on an application, a panel of biomarkers, or a clinic promising rejuvenation, with no common framework against which any of it can be read.

The commercial layer is already substantial. Direct to consumer epigenetic age tests are now sold online, longevity clinics offering biological age panels have opened in many cities, and consumer wearables report readiness, recovery, and pace of aging scores derived from proprietary and largely undisclosed algorithms. None of these products share a common scale, none is obliged to demonstrate that its output responds to intervention, and a person who buys two of them may receive two different biological ages with no means of reconciling them. This is the environment into which any public facing instrument would arrive, and it is why such an instrument is worth building and not merely describing.

Cardiovascular medicine encountered a comparable problem and resolved it not with a new therapeutic but with a communication instrument: Life's Essential 8, which distilled a contested risk landscape into eight components scored from 0 to 100, and which has since been shown to track biological aging itself. This perspective argues that geroscience has assembled much of the material for an equivalent instrument, even while the field continues to disagree about foundational questions. Expert panels have converged on which biomarkers are worth tracking as outcomes in aging intervention trials, and have concluded that no single biomarker suffices, which leaves a composite as the only viable path. What has not happened is the translation of that research-level agreement into a public-facing instrument.

Dendritic Cell Antigen Presentation Enables T Cells to Enter the Brain and Contribute to Tau Pathology https://www.fightaging.org/archives/2026/09/dendritic-cell-antigen-presentation-enables-t-cells-to-enter-the-brain-and-contribute-to-tau-pathology/

The immune systems of the body and brain are distinct and separate, or at least largely separate, influencing one another via signaling. The blood-brain barrier keeps the vast majority of immune cells in the body out of the brain, and vice versa. A few channels have been discovered in recent years whereby a small number of adaptive immune cells, such as T cells, enter the brain in the normal course of events. Additionally, the blood-brain barrier becomes dysfunctional and leaky with age, allowing a wide range of unwanted cells into the brain, T cells included.

Increasing inflammatory activity in the innate immune cells of the brain known as microglia is a growing focus of research interest in the context of aging and neurodegenerative conditions. While some of of this maladaptive behavior arises from reactions to local conditions and internal age-related damage, some is driven by interactions with the body's immune system. Along the way, attention has also turned to the entry of T cells into the brain, and their potential role in provoking inflammatory neurodegeneration. In today's open access paper, for example, researchers demonstrate that dendritic cells encourage T cells to enter the brain to cause problems. Removing the dendritic cells in mice reduces the impact of T cells on the aging of the brain and progression of neurodegeneration.
Priming of CD8+ T cells by peripheral dendritic cells exacerbates tau-mediated neurodegeneration

Tauopathies are a group of neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer's disease and certain forms of frontotemporal dementia, defined by the intracellular aggregation of hyperphosphorylated tau protein, which tightly correlates with neuronal dysfunction and death. Tauopathy is accompanied by increased reactive microglia and astrocytes and increased T cells in the brain, particularly CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes. We previously found that depleting T cells significantly ameliorated tau-mediated neurodegeneration in p.Pro301Ser (P301S) tau transgenic mice expressing human APOE4 (TE4), supporting an active role for T cells in driving tau-mediated neurodegeneration.

Clonally expanded CD8+ T cells constituted a majority of the infiltrating CD3+ T cells (~60-70%) in TE4 brain. Conventional type 1 dendritic cell (cDC1s) are specialized antigen-presenting cells (APCs) that perform antigen cross-presentation, a process that involves presenting exogenously derived antigens on major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC-I) molecules to prime CD8+ T cells. During T cell priming, naive CD8+ T cells receive antigenic, co-stimulatory and cytokine signals from APCs, driving their differentiation into effector cells that subsequently migrate to peripheral tissues to execute their immune functions.

Here, we investigated the role of cDC1s in tau-mediated neurodegeneration by genetically ablating cDC1s or disrupting their antigen cross-presentation capacity in TE4 mice. Both interventions markedly protected against neurodegeneration and selectively reduced CD8+ T cell accumulation in the brain. Importantly, we found that cDC1-dependent antigen cross-presentation of a brain-derived antigen occurs outside central nervous system tissues, highlighting peripheral antigen presentation as a potential therapeutic target for tauopathies, including Alzheimer's disease.
Sizable Declines in Associative Memory Occur by Age 50 https://www.fightaging.org/archives/2026/09/sizable-declines-in-associative-memory-occur-by-age-50/

Some aspects of cognitive function exhibit marked declines relatively early in later life, by middle age. Here, researchers show that episodic and associative memory recall, meaning the ability to correctly link together and place in context specific individual memories, shows a sizable decline in 50-something participants versus their 20-something counterparts. The fine details of the storage of memories are understood to be fairly dynamic over time; accessing memory can change storage, as can mechanisms of aging operating on the organization of neural networks. Even outside the context of aging, memory is far from perfect even in the best of circumstances. We forget most of our personal histories quite quickly, retaining perhaps 2% of the past according to early research into memory and forgetting. There is a great deal of room for improvement.

Episodic memory is the ability to bind elements of an experience into coherent associations. This ability declines with age, often producing errors that can interfere with daily life. Memory distortions might arise from unstable hippocampal representations that cannot be maintained across encoding, storage, and later retrieval. However, whether aging disrupts the temporal continuity of these representations across memory phases has not been directly tested.

Here, adults aged 20-74 completed functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) scanning during an associative memory task involving face-object and face-scene pairings, followed by post-encoding rest and a cued retrieval test. Using multivoxel correlation structure analyses, we quantified hippocampal pattern similarity across each memory stage. Increasing age was associated with increased category errors and reduced representational similarity across all transitions. Higher encoding-retrieval similarity predicted better associative accuracy in younger adults and was less predictive in middle-aged and diminished in older adults.

Uniquely among older adults, greater cross-phase similarity predicted elevated category-level binding errors, suggesting a shift from selective reactivation to misbinding with age. Baseline hippocampal organization and encoding-specific connectivity supported accurate reinstatement only in younger adults. Thus aging disrupts hippocampal stability, possibly representing a core mechanism of age-related decline in associative memory across the adult lifespan.
Engineered Exosomes as a Treatment for Alzheimer's Disease https://www.fightaging.org/archives/2026/09/engineered-exosomes-as-a-treatment-for-alzheimers-disease/

Exosomes are one category of extracellular vesicle secreted by cells, a membrane-wrapped package of molecules, one complex component of the extensive, incompletely mapped communication that takes place constantly between cells. Exosome therapies are conceptually similar to stem cell therapies, an attempt to favorably adjust the behavior of native cells via signaling. While the first exosome therapies are widely available via medical tourism, with a few organizations in the early stages of sponsoring clinical trials to allow use in more regulated regions, the research community is assessing approaches that involve engineering the contents or surface features of exosomes harvested from young donor blood, tissues, or stem cells. The example here is tested in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease, producing favorable results.

In this study, the rabies virus glycoprotein-targeting peptide (RVG-29) was conjugated to the surface of young plasma-derived exosomes (EXOs) to construct RVG-engineered EXOs (RVG-EXOs). RVG-EXOs exhibit enhanced blood-brain barrier penetration and neuron targeting, thus offering an efficient delivery system for targeted Alzheimer's disease (AD) therapy. RVG-EXOs treatment markedly improved multiple cognitive behaviors in 3xTg AD mice, including spatial learning, working memory, and novel object recognition. RVG-EXOs effectively alleviated AD pathology by promoting amyloid-β clearance, suppressing Tau hyperphosphorylation, and preserving synaptic integrity and neuronal survival.

Mechanistic studies revealed that RVG-EXOs activates the autophagy pathway by inhibiting RPTOR expression, providing a molecular basis for the neuroprotective effects of young plasma exosomes. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed that RVG-EXOs remodeled brain cellular landscape: increased neurons, rebalanced inhibitory/excitatory neurons, strengthened Ptn-Sdc3 neuroprotection, and attenuated APP-CD74 signaling, which suppressed disease-associated microglia (DAM) and promoted homeostatic microglia.

Age Acceleration in Various Proteomic Clocks Correlates with Risk of Mortality and Age-Related Disease https://www.fightaging.org/archives/2026/09/age-acceleration-in-various-proteomic-clocks-correlates-with-risk-of-mortality-and-age-related-disease/

In recent years, researchers have been gathering as much data as possible on the behavior of aging clocks of various sorts. The study here is an example of the type, in which multiple proteomic clocks were assessed in large epidemiological study populations. As one might expect, where there is age acceleration, meaning a higher clock age than chronological age, this correlates with a greater risk of age-related disease and mortality. Though as noted, clocks don't improve all that much on lifestyle indicators when it comes to the quality of the correlation. This sort of study helps to build a foundation of data as a reference for further exploration of clock behavior in response to interventions thought to affect the pace or state of degenerative aging.

Assessment of biological aging using proteomic clocks may enhance risk prediction and elucidate the molecular links between aging and chronic diseases. Here, among 17,473 participants of the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition, we examined associations of plasma SomaScan-based proteomic clocks, including organ-specific clocks, with risk factors, 24 incident chronic diseases and all-cause mortality, over up to 28 years of follow-up. Replication was conducted in the Whitehall II study.

We show that the global age gap, an age acceleration score combining proteomic clocks, was associated with smoking, alcohol consumption, physical inactivity and higher risk of mortality, cardiovascular diseases, dementia and cancers of the liver, upper aero-digestive tract, lung and kidney. Lung, kidney and stomach cancers were more strongly associated with related organ-specific age gaps. Predictive performance of proteomic clocks for mortality was comparable to that of classical lifestyle risk factors. In summary, proteomic clocks appear promising biomarkers of generalized age-related disease risk.
Dogs Exhibit Comorbidity and Mortality Risk in Much the Same Way as Humans https://www.fightaging.org/archives/2026/09/dogs-exhibit-comorbidity-and-mortality-risk-in-much-the-same-way-as-humans/

One of the goals of the Dog Aging Project is to better establish that the characteristics of aging in dogs are close enough to the characteristics of aging in humans to make the results of interventions on dog life span relevant to the development of human medicine. Thus the paper here, in which researchers establish that comorbidity, the presence of multiple age-related conditions in the same individual, has much the same relationship with aging and mortality in dogs as it does in people. To have an age-related disease is to have a significant degree of dysfunction in some organ or tissue. The greater the burden of underlying cell and tissue damage resulting from aging, the more likely it is that multiple age-related conditions will emerge. Further, significant dysfunction in any one organ or tissue will tend to generate issues in other organs or tissues; everything connections everything else in our biology.

Multimorbidity, the presence of two or more conditions, is associated with a higher risk of death as individuals age. However, modeling multimorbidity in laboratory animals is difficult, if not impossible, because specific conditions are seldom individually diagnosed and treated in these settings. Because of their shared environment, physiology, and genetic diversity, and because they are medically managed as individuals, companion dogs have potential to serve as a translational multimorbidity model. Yet it is unknown how diagnoses accumulate over time, how these diagnoses are associated with mortality, and which multimorbid condition combinations are the most prevalent and hazardous.

Utilizing owner-reported data from over 50,000 dogs in the Dog Aging Project (DAP), we assessed how multimorbidities develop, learned which are the most prevalent, and evaluated their impact on survival. Like in humans, we show that the accumulation of conditions is associated with an increased risk of death in dogs. We also present data suggesting that future reported condition rates vary depending on the conditions a dog's owner already has reported. Not surprisingly, our analysis reveals that the overall canine aging process appears to be the driving factor behind disease development, more so than other covariates. Through classifying multimorbidities, we found that almost all either exhibit a synergistic effect or are driven by a single, predominant condition. In both cases, osteoarthritis, overweight, and cancer were highly prevalent throughout.
This analysis expands on previously conducted DAP work and further highlights the usefulness of the companion dog as a translational model for human aging.

Automation of Screening Studies for Compounds that Slow Aging is Becoming More Ambitious https://www.fightaging.org/archives/2026/09/automation-of-screening-studies-for-compounds-that-slow-aging-is-becoming-more-ambitious/

Screening compound libraries for effects on aging in short-lived species has grown to become a significant area of interest in the aging research community. As a general rule, discoveries are modest in effect size, and largely take the form of novel ways to influence the beneficial maintenance and repair activities (such as autophagy) triggered by calorie restriction, heat, cold, and other forms of stress. These responses have a much larger effect on life span in short-lived species than in long-lived species, so in the long run are not all that interesting. Nonetheless, considerable effort has been made to find ways to make this screening process more efficient and automated. Research equipment has been constructed to house tens of thousands of nematode worms and use machine learning analysis of imagery to report on measures of health. Many of the techniques involved have been attempted in mouse studies to at least some degree. Here find an example of the state of the art in this type of work.

bodyOriginal.text: Six different aging clocks detected younger blood protein profiles in patients taking the experimental lung-fibrosis drug rentosertib. This suggests possible anti-aging effects, but separating those from the narrower benefits of treating fibrosis remains a challenge [1].

The AI-developed drug Many drugs developed for particular diseases act on aging-related biological processes. That creates an opportunity: a clinical trial could investigate both whether a drug treats its intended disease and whether it has broader effects on aging. Ordinary clinical measurements cannot establish those broader effects, but we now have biological age clocks that closely track chronological age or predict mortality risk [2]. These clocks have been used in numerous trials as proxies to estimate the intervention’s effect on aging.

In a new study published in Nature Biotechnology , the researchers analyzed blood samples from a Phase 2a trial whose results were published last year [3]. That 12-week, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial tested rentosertib, an inhibitor of the kinase TNIK, which has been implicated in several aging-related processes [4].

Rentosertib was developed by the longevity biotech company Insilico, using a proprietary AI-based drug discovery platform, to treat idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), a progressive disease in which excessive scar tissue compromises lung function. IPF is age-related, with a mean age of onset around 65 years, and aging processes such as cellular senescence and inflammation are heavily involved.
The new analysis included 42 of the trial’s 71 participants. Alongside placebo, the trial tested three regimens: 30 milligrams once daily, 30 milligrams twice daily, and 60 milligrams once daily.

Lower biological age readings The researchers used six different proteomic clocks, which analyze protein levels in blood. The proteomic clocks’ appeal is partly interpretability: researchers can identify which proteins affect the readings and connect them to known biological processes more directly than is often possible with methylation-based clocks. The clocks were developed by different teams, using data from UK Biobank, including one clock developed by Insilico itself. Four of the clocks were trained on chronological age, and two on mortality.

All six clocks detected lower predicted biological ages in patients taking rentosertib, although not at every dose or visit. After four weeks, the four chronological age-based clocks rated patients taking 60 milligrams once daily (the single-dose regimen) roughly three years younger, on average, than at the start of treatment. These changes were statistically significant compared with placebo. However, the two clocks trained to predict mortality risk did not show a significant change at that dose at week four.

Patients taking 30 milligrams twice daily (the split-dose regimen) showed the most consistent decreases across both types of clocks. The largest reductions in predicted biological age appeared by week four, with little additional change over the remaining eight weeks.

These results essentially mean that patients’ blood protein profiles became more similar to those associated with younger people. They do not, however, establish that the treated patients regained years of youth or would live longer.

Is there a broad anti-aging effect? Looking beyond the clock readings, the researchers found that treatment changed the levels of 326 blood proteins, including proteins involved in fibrosis, metabolism, and cellular stress responses. Most changes in the two higher-dose groups persisted throughout the trial or appeared later in treatment, suggesting that the drug continued affecting patients’ biology even after predicted ages plateaued.

The researchers then examined which proteins contributed most to the younger age estimates. A fibrosis-associated protein, LTBP2, stood out as a major contributor. It was used by all six clocks, which raises the question of whether their agreement mainly reflects the drug’s effect on fibrosis, rather than broader slowing of aging.

To explore whether the lower age estimates reflected more than improvement in fibrosis, the researchers compared changes in predicted age with changes in lung function. The two did not closely track each other. This suggests that improved lung function alone might not explain the clock changes, although lung function does not capture every aspect of IPF.

The team then compared the treatment-induced protein changes with differences between younger and older participants in UK Biobank. With the split dose, proteins associated with aging tended to move in the opposite direction: those found at higher levels in older people tended to decrease, and vice versa. This pattern was not statistically significant with the single daily dose.

Finally, the researchers examined proteins associated with cellular senescence. These proteins tended to increase in the placebo group but decrease with treatment, suggesting that rentosertib might reduce senescence-associated activity, although the researchers did not directly measure senescent cells in tissues.

These findings strengthen the case for investigating rentosertib as a potential geroprotector. However, because fibrosis, metabolism, and senescence are closely connected, they still cannot definitively establish whether the drug affects aging beyond its benefits for IPF.

“This study illustrates how biomarkers of aging can be incorporated into conventional clinical trials,” Vadim Gladyshev, a professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School and a coauthor of the study, told Lifespan News. “If validated more broadly, such approaches could allow us to learn not only whether a treatment affects a particular disease, but also whether it influences some aspects of aging biology.”

articles.titleOriginal: Genflow’s gene therapy lowers biological age markers in aged dogs
articles.summaryOriginal: A SIRT6 gene therapy trial in senior beagles hit its primary endpoint, lowering biological age and offering a test bed for human medicine. Old dogs make surprisingly good stand-ins for aging humans. They live in our homes, eat roughly what we eat, breathe the same air and develop many of the same age-related conditions we […] The post Genflow’s gene therapy lowers biological age markers in aged do

bodyOriginal.text: A SIRT6 gene therapy trial in senior beagles hit its primary endpoint, lowering biological age and offering a test bed for human medicine.

Old dogs make surprisingly good stand-ins for aging humans. They live in our homes, eat roughly what we eat, breathe the same air and develop many of the same age-related conditions we do, just on a faster timeline. That’s part of why a UK biotech’s just-announced results from a beagle trial are getting attention well beyond the veterinary world.

Genflow Biosciences announced that its SLAB clinical trial, short for Sarcopenia and Longevity in Aged Beagles, has met its primary endpoint. The study tested the company’s SIRT6 centenarian gene therapy in dogs over the age of 10, and the treated animals showed a clear reduction in biological age compared with untreated controls, as measured by the GRIM DNA methylation clock, one of the more established tools researchers use to estimate how “old” tissue actually behaves, independent of a subject’s birthdate [ 1 ].
Borrowing biology from people who live past 100

Genflow’s approach centers on a specific variant of the SIRT6 gene, a version found more often in centenarians than in the general population, that appears to help protect cells against age-related decline. The company’s lead compound, GF-1002, delivers this centenarian variant directly, aiming to nudge aging tissue back toward a younger functional state rather than simply managing symptoms.

The trial itself was randomized and blinded, splitting 24 beagles over age 10 into four groups: two cohorts receiving naked DNA treatment at different doses, one group getting a single dose delivered via an AAV8 viral vector, and a saline control group. Hitting the primary endpoint builds on earlier signals the company had already flagged, including positive interim muscle data reported back in February and confirmation of sustained safety and efficacy at a three-month follow-up in April.

Beyond the headline result, Genflow says treated dogs showed improvement across several secondary functional and observable measures, too, though the company is holding the detailed breakdown for the Animal Longevity Summit (ALOS) in Toronto on 1–2 October. It’s a notable venue choice: ALOS bills itself as the first conference built entirely around animal longevity, and its speaker list, including researchers like Matt Kaeberlein, Vera Gorbunova and Aubrey de Grey, reads like a who’s who of the broader anti-aging research world. That overlap isn’t a coincidence. Companion animal trials are increasingly seen as a faster, more naturalistic proving ground for interventions that could eventually make their way to humans.

“Meeting the primary endpoint in SLAB is a defining milestone for Genflow,” said Dr Eric Leire, the company’s CEO. “We set out to demonstrate that our centenarian SIRT6 naked DNA therapy could measurably address age-related decline in a real-world aging mode. This provides a powerful foundation for our partner discussions across animal health. We look forward to sharing the full dataset, including the critical methylation clock and muscle histology results, with the scientific and investment communities at the Animal Longevity Summit in October.”
Dr Eric Leire, founder and CEO of Genflow Biosciences

That mention of partner discussions is worth noting. Genflow says it’s in active conversations with major global animal health companies about licensing and commercialization, which would be the fastest realistic route to market for a therapy like this: getting it into veterinary use for aging pets before the much longer road toward human regulatory approval.

Founded in 2020 and headquartered in the UK with R&D operations in Belgium, Genflow has built its pipeline entirely around age-related disease. Beyond the SIRT6 program in dogs, the company is exploring GF-1002 as a potential treatment for MASH, a common and stubborn form of liver disease, and developing a separate mRNA-based SIRT6 therapy, GF-1006, aimed at corneal disease and glaucoma.

Dogs won’t tell us everything about how a therapy like this behaves in people, and a successful trial in beagles is several steps removed from anything a human patient could access. However, sarcopenia, the muscle loss that comes with age, is one of the more universal and disabling parts of getting older, in dogs and people alike. A therapy that measurably slows it, even in a 24-dog trial, is the kind of early proof point the longevity field has been short on.

articles.titleOriginal: SCI model takes longevity beyond the clinic
articles.summaryOriginal: APLMS will use Singapore, China and India to test how longevity science can translate into function, prevention and healthier lives at scale. The Asia-Pacific Longevity Medicine Society (APLMS) is developing a regional model intended to move healthy longevity out of specialist settings and into everyday life, using Singapore, China and India as distinct environments in […] The post SCI model takes

bodyOriginal.text: APLMS will use Singapore, China and India to test how longevity science can translate into function, prevention and healthier lives at scale.

The Asia-Pacific Longevity Medicine Society (APLMS) is developing a regional model intended to move healthy longevity out of specialist settings and into everyday life, using Singapore, China and India as distinct environments in which to generate real-world evidence and test approaches to prevention. Its scope is substantial: the three countries together represent approximately 2.8 billion people – more than a third of the world’s population – but population size is only part of the proposition.

Hong Kong hosts the model’s public debut: APLMS will introduce and further develop SCI at the 2026 Asia-Pacific Healthy Longevity International Summit , running 1–4 October. The questions on the table are deceptively simple – what travels across cultures and healthcare systems, what needs reinventing locally, and whether any of this actually changes outcomes once it leaves the laboratory or the specialist clinic.

Longevity.Technology: Longevity medicine has become increasingly sophisticated at measuring aging; the more important test is whether those measurements translate into lives with more function, independence and resilience – and fewer years constrained by chronic disease. A biomarker can tell us something fascinating about aging biology; it cannot carry the shopping upstairs. The SCI model’s emphasis on real-world evidence across very different populations is therefore interesting, particularly because it treats technology as a means rather than the endpoint. Longevity medicine that stays confined to the premium clinic is, in the end, a hobby for the wealthy rather than a population-health strategy; its useful interventions have to find their way into ordinary healthcare, workplaces and communities, or they don’t much matter. That journey looks different in Singapore, China and India, and assuming otherwise – that what works in one population will travel neatly to another – is precisely the kind of assumption SCI is built to test rather than indulge. The arithmetic alone should focus the mind: at a scale of some 2.8 billion people, even a modest gain in functional health stops being modest. The interesting question is whether they can be demonstrated – then delivered.

The thinking owes something to blue zones – those pockets of the world where people seem to age unusually well. What’s striking about many of them, on APLMS’s account, is the absence of anything exceptional: no particular wealth, no advanced healthcare, just ordinary people living ordinary lives amid strong daily habits, social bonds and cultural continuity that happen to compound rather well over decades. Whether that pattern generalizes is precisely the question SCI intends to test, rather than assume.

APLMS has selected Singapore, China and India precisely because they are not interchangeable. Singapore combines established public-health infrastructure and population-based healthcare with research in geroscience and precision medicine; its multicultural population and emphasis on prevention offer one environment in which longevity approaches can be evaluated in practice.

China – the world’s second-largest economy, home to more than 1.4 billion people – brings scale of a different order, alongside growing digital-health capabilities and extensive experience in population health. Its healthcare landscape also encompasses both modern medicine and longstanding culturally rooted health practices, providing another test of what translation means when scientific evidence meets existing behaviors and systems of care.

India, now the world’s most populous country, adds considerable heterogeneity in diet, culture, family structures and community life. APLMS also points to Ayurveda and its emphasis on daily routines, nutrition, sleep, physical activity and mental wellbeing; these traditions will sit alongside India’s developing scientific, healthcare and digital-health capabilities within the proposed model.

The intention is not to identify a single cultural recipe for longevity. Quite the reverse: SCI is conceived as an evidence-led translation network capable of separating principles that prove transferable from those that remain stubbornly local.

Central to the model is a shift in emphasis from surrogate measures toward function. Aging biology and biomarkers remain important, as do digital tools and emerging interventions; APLMS argues, however, that their value should ultimately be judged against mobility, independence, chronic disease burden, wellbeing and disability-free years.

That distinction matters. Longevity research increasingly has access to exquisitely granular measurements of biological processes, yet a statistically interesting movement in a biomarker does not automatically confer a clinically meaningful benefit. Function is messier. It is also difficult to ignore.

SCI will therefore look beyond what happens during a clinical encounter to the conditions accumulated over decades – diet and movement, certainly, but also social connection, environment, purpose, community participation and access to preventive care. Medicine and technology are positioned as tools for understanding, measuring and strengthening those foundations rather than substitutes for them.

The real-world evidence component is where the model becomes more ambitious. Controlled studies remain essential for establishing efficacy and safety, but population health has an inconvenient habit of taking place under uncontrolled conditions – among different diets, healthcare infrastructures, socioeconomic circumstances and cultural expectations.

APLMS plans to establish an SCI Healthy Longevity Real-World Evidence and Translation Network, with initial work during 2026–27 expected to include a shared framework and pragmatic common outcomes, alongside opportunities for real-world studies, clinician education and implementation pathways.

A dedicated session at the Hong Kong summit – titled The SCI Healthy Longevity Model: Everyday Life, Real-World Evidence and Prevention at Scale – will begin that process, bringing together researchers, clinicians, healthcare leaders and implementation partners. The challenge will be to preserve enough methodological consistency to make findings useful while allowing sufficient local flexibility to make them relevant – scale without context is not quite scale.

Perhaps the larger proposition is where SCI ultimately intends its findings to go. APLMS explicitly envisages pathways beyond premium longevity clinics and wellness services, extending evidence-based approaches into communities, workplaces, employers, insurers and established health systems.

That is a considerably tougher translational problem than offering another test or intervention to an already engaged longevity consumer. Prevention at population level must contend with accessibility, adherence, cultural acceptability and healthcare economics; what is biologically plausible must also become practically usable.

APLMS President Dr Tim Shi frames the ambition in much the same terms. The model, he said, is not intended to create another theoretical framework or search for a single formula for aging; its purpose is “to build a practical, culturally relevant, scientifically credible and scalable model, validated through real-world evidence and translated into better prevention, healthier everyday living and ultimately better health outcomes.”
Asia-Pacific, in that sense, offers an unusually large arena in which to attempt that work – diverse, rapidly aging and far too heterogeneous for easy answers.

If SCI develops as intended, its value may lie less in producing another definition of healthy longevity than in discovering which ideas remain useful when exposed to billions of complicated, ordinary lives. That is where prevention has to work eventually.
The 2026 Asia-Pacific Healthy Longevity International Summit is 1–4 October 2026 at The Hopewell Hotel in Hong Kong – to find out more CLICK HERE .

articles.titleKo: SCI 모델은 임상을 넘어 롱제비티를 가져갑니다
articles.summaryKo: APLMS는 싱가포르, 중국, 인도를 활용해 롱제비티 과학이 기능, 예방, 그리고 대규모 건강한 삶으로 어떻게 전환될 수 있는지 시험할 예정입니다. 아시아-태평양 롱제비티 의학회(APLMS)는 싱가포르, 중국, 인도를 독립된 환경으로 활용하여 건강한 롱제비티를 일상생활로 확장하는 지역 모델을 개발 중입니다. 포스트 SCI 모델은
bodyKo: APLMS는 싱가포르, 중국, 인도를 활용해 롱제비티 과학이 기능, 예방, 그리고 대규모 건강한 삶으로 어떻게 이어질 수 있는지 시험할 예정입니다.

아시아-태평양 롱제비티 의학회(APLMS)는 싱가포르, 중국, 인도를 각각 실제 증거를 생성하고 예방 접근법을 시험하는 독립된 환경으로 활용하여 건강한 롱제비티를 일상생활로 확장하는 지역 모델을 개발 중입니다. 이 계획의 범위는 상당하며, 세 나라를 합쳐 약 28억 명, 즉 전 세계 인구의 3분의 1 이상을 차지하지만, 인구 규모는 전체 제안의 일부에 불과합니다.

홍콩에서 이 모델의 공개 데뷔가 이루어집니다: APLMS는 2026년 아시아-태평양 건강롱제비티 국제 정상회의(10월 1일부터 4일까지 열림)에서 SCI를 소개하고 더욱 발전시킬 예정입니다. 논의 중인 질문들은 겉보기에는 단순합니다 – 문화와 의료 시스템을 넘나드는 것, 현지에서 재창조해야 할 것, 그리고 이 모든 것이 실험실이나 전문 클리닉을 떠난 후 실제로 결과를 바꿀 수 있는지.

롱제비티. 기술: 롱제비티 의학은 노화 측정에 점점 더 정교해졌다; 더 중요한 시험은 이러한 측정이 더 많은 기능, 독립성, 회복력을 가진 삶으로 이어지는지, 그리고 만성 질환에 시달리는 기간이 줄어들지에 대한 것이다. 바이오마커는 노화 생물학에 대해 흥미로운 것을 알려줄 수 있다; 하지만 쇼핑을 위층으로 가져다줄 수는 없다. SCI 모델이 매우 다른 인구에 걸쳐 실제 증거를 강조하는 점은 특히 기술을 종착지가 아닌 수단으로 다루기 때문에 흥미롭다. 프리미엄 클리닉에만 국한된 롱제비티 의학은 결국 부유층의 취미에 불과하며, 인구 건강 전략이 아니다; 유용한 개입이 일반 의료, 직장, 지역사회에 도입되지 않으면 별로 중요하지 않다. 싱가포르, 중국, 인도에서는 그 여정이 다르게 보이며, 그렇지 않다고 가정하는 — 한 집단에서 효과가 다른 집단에 깔끔하게 전달될 것이라고 가정하는 것은 SCI가 시험하기 위해 만들어진 전제다. 산수만으로도 마음을 집중시켜야 한다: 약 28억 명의 인구 규모에서는 기능적 건강의 소소한 향상조차도 결코 미미하지 않는다. 흥미로운 질문은 그것들이 입증되고 — 그리고 실현될 수 있느냐 하는 것이다.

이러한 사고방식은 블루존, 즉 사람들이 유난히 나이를 잘 드는 지역에서 어느 정도 빚지고 있습니다. APLMS의 설명에 따르면, 많은 블루존에서 눈에 띄는 점은 특별한 것이 없다는 것입니다. 특별한 부도, 첨단 의료도 없이, 단지 평범한 사람들이 수십 년에 걸쳐 쌓아온 강한 일상 습관, 사회적 유대, 문화적 연속성 속에서 평범한 삶을 살아가는 것입니다. 이 패턴이 일반화되는지는 SCI가 가정하기보다는 검증하려는 바로 질문입니다.
APLMS는 싱가포르, 중국, 인도를 선택한 이유가 바로 이들이 상호 교환 가능하지 않기 때문입니다. 싱가포르는 확립된 공중보건 인프라와 인구 기반 의료를 노인과학 및 정밀 의학 연구와 결합하고 있습니다; 다문화 인구와 예방에 대한 강조는 롱제비티 접근법을 실천에서 평가할 수 있는 한 가지 환경을 제공합니다.
중국은 세계에서 두 번째로 큰 경제 대국으로, 14억 명이 넘는 인구를 보유하고 있으며, 디지털 헬스 역량 증가와 인구 건강 분야의 폭넓은 경험을 더해 다른 차원의 규모를 제공합니다. 중국의 의료 환경은 현대 의학과 오랜 문화적 전통을 모두 포함하여, 과학적 증거가 기존 행동과 치료 체계와 만날 때 번역이 무엇을 의미하는지 또 다른 시험대를 제공합니다.
현재 세계에서 인구가 가장 많은 인도는 식단, 문화, 가족 구조, 공동체 생활 면에서 상당한 이질성을 더하고 있습니다. APLMS는 또한 아유르베다와 그 일상 루틴, 영양, 수면, 신체 활동, 정신 건강에 대한 강조를 강조합니다; 이러한 전통들은 제안된 모델 내에서 인도의 과학, 의료 및 디지털 건강 역량 발전과 함께 공존할 것입니다.
의도는 롱제비티를 위한 단일 문화적 레시피를 찾는 것이 아닙니다. 오히려 반대입니다: SCI는 전이 가능한 원칙과 완강히 지역에만 머무는 원칙을 분리할 수 있는 증거 중심의 번역 네트워크로 구상됩니다.
이 모델의 핵심은 대체 측정에서 기능으로의 강조 전환입니다. 노화된 생물학과 바이오마커는 여전히 중요하며, 디지털 도구와 신흥 개입도 마찬가지입니다; 그러나 APLMS는 이러한 가치는 궁극적으로 이동성, 독립성, 만성 질환 부담, 웰빙, 장애 없는 시기와 비교해 평가되어야 한다고 주장합니다.
그 구분은 중요합니다. 롱제비티 연구는 점점 더 세밀한 생물학적 과정을 측정할 수 있게 되었지만, 바이오마커의 통계적으로 흥미로운 움직임이 반드시 임상적으로 의미 있는 이익을 가져오지는 않습니다. 기능은 더 복잡합니다. 또한 무시하기도 어렵습니다.
따라서 SCI는 임상 진료 과정에서 일어나는 일을 넘어 수십 년에 걸쳐 축적된 조건들—물론 식습관과 움직임뿐 아니라 사회적 연결, 환경, 목적, 지역사회 참여, 예방 치료 접근성—에도 관심을 보입니다. 의학과 기술은 이러한 기초를 이해하고 측정하며 강화하는 도구로 자리매김하며, 대체물이 아닙니다.
실제 증거 요소에서 모델이 더 야심차게 됩니다. 통제된 연구는 효능과 안전성을 입증하는 데 필수적이지만, 인구 건강은 다양한 식단, 의료 인프라, 사회경제적 상황, 문화적 기대 등 통제되지 않은 환경에서 이루어지는 불편한 경향이 있습니다.
APLMS는 SCI 건강한 롱제비티 실세계 근거 및 번역 네트워크를 구축할 계획이며, 2026–27년 초기 작업은 공유 프레임워크와 실용적 공통 결과, 그리고 실제 연구 기회, 임상가 교육, 실행 경로 제공을 포함할 예정입니다.

홍콩 정상회의에서 열리는 전용 세션인 'SCI 건강한 롱제비티 모델: 일상생활, 실제 증거 및 대규모 예방'이 이 과정을 시작하며, 연구자, 임상의, 의료 리더 및 실행 파트너를 한자리에 모을 것입니다. 과제는 연구 결과를 유용하게 만들기 위해 충분한 방법론적 일관성을 유지하면서도, 지역적 유연성을 충분히 허용해 관련성을 높이는 것입니다 – 맥락 없는 규모는 완전한 규모가 아닙니다.
아마도 더 큰 제안이 SCI가 궁극적으로 연구 결과를 향하도록 의도하는 방향일 것입니다. APLMS는 프리미엄 롱제비티 클리닉과 웰니스 서비스를 넘어 지역사회, 직장, 고용주, 보험사 및 기존 보건 시스템으로 근거 기반 접근법을 확장하는 경로를 명확히 구상합니다.
이는 이미 참여하는 롱제비티 소비자에게 또 다른 검사나 개입을 제공하는 것보다 훨씬 더 어려운 번역 문제입니다. 인구 수준에서의 예방은 접근성, 준수, 문화적 수용성, 의료 경제성과 경쟁해야 하며; 생물학적으로 그럴듯한 것이 실질적으로 사용 가능해져야 합니다.

APLMS 회장 팀 시 박사도 이 목표를 비슷한 방식으로 제시합니다. 그는 이 모델이 또 다른 이론적 틀을 만들거나 노화에 대한 단일 공식을 찾으려는 것이 아니라고 말했습니다; 그 목적은 "실용적이고 문화적으로 관련성 있으며 과학적으로 신뢰할 수 있고 확장 가능한 모델을 구축하고, 실제 세계의 증거를 통해 검증되어 더 나은 예방, 더 건강한 일상생활, 궁극적으로 더 나은 건강 결과로 전환하는 것"이라고 말했습니다.
그런 의미에서 아시아 태평양은 그 작업을 시도하기에 이례적으로 큰 무대를 제공한다 – 다양하고 빠르게 고화되고 있으며 너무 이질적이어서 쉽게 답하기 어렵다.
만약 SCI가 의도한 대로 발달한다면, 그 가치는 건강한 롱제비티의 또 다른 정의를 만드는 데 있기보다는, 수십억 명의 복잡하고 평범한 삶에 노출되었을 때 어떤 아이디어가 여전히 유용한지 발견하는 데 있을 수 있습니다. 결국 예방이 반드시 작동해야 할 부분이 바로 그 부분입니다.
2026년 아시아-태평양 건강롱제비티 국제 정상회의는 2026년 10월 1일부터 4일까지 홍콩 호프웰 호텔에서 열립니다 – 자세한 내용은 여기를 클릭하세요.
"SCI 모델이 임상을 넘어 롱제비티를 넘어 롱제비티"라는 글이 처음 게재되었습니다. 기술.

bodyOriginal.text: Outer Bio’s Yuna platform keeps living human skin functioning for a month, a longer window for testing what actually slows visible aging.

Cut a piece of human skin out of the body, and the clock starts ticking. Within days, it stops behaving like skin at all. The cells that once fought inflammation, rebuilt collagen and healed wounds start to shut down. For the scientists trying to figure out which compounds actually slow skin aging, that short window has always been the problem. You can’t watch a process that takes weeks to unfold if your test tissue is dead before week one even ends.

A new company thinks it has cracked that particular puzzle. Outer Bio came out of stealth this week with a platform called Yuna, which keeps full-thickness human skin (epidermis, dermis, immune cells and all) alive and testable for a full four weeks [ 1 ]. That’s long enough, the company says, to watch the slow biological processes behind aging skin actually happen in real time, in real human tissue.

Skincare is a more than $100 billion industry, and yet in three decades of research, only one topical ingredient (here’s looking at you, retinoids) has earned FDA recognition for visibly improving aging skin.

Outer Bio’s pitch is that this isn’t for lack of trying or lack of money. It’s a technical bottleneck. The biology that matters for aging skin – how collagen rebuilds itself, how chronic low-grade inflammation (“inflammaging,” as longevity researchers have taken to calling it) does its damage, how senescent cells pile up and stop functioning – takes weeks to play out. Standard lab skin can’t survive that long, so researchers have effectively been asked to judge a marathon by watching the first hundred yards.

Yuna is built to remove that constraint. The tissue comes from donors spanning different ages, sexes, and skin tones, and it’s tracked continuously for the full month. Cell activity, tissue structure and protein signals. Each compound tested generates more than 30,000 data points, and the company says it has already amassed over 10 terabytes of data from more than 300 donors and 10,000 individual treatments.

The living-tissue data is designed to feed a machine-learning system that gets smarter with every test. Models trained on Yuna’s results help prioritize which compounds to try next, and each new result sharpens the next prediction. Outer Bio says its virtual screening library already covers 5.9 million compounds, with plans to eventually work through libraries in the billions.

“Skincare has never lacked demand or ambition. It has lacked the ability to study compounds and mechanisms in living human skin over a biologically relevant timeframe,” said Michael Polansky, co-founder and CEO of Outer Bio. “Most experimental platforms rely on reconstructed skin or cell monolayers. Those models can tell you whether a compound is toxic; they can’t tell you whether it works, because they lack the complexity and architecture of the real organ. And they fail within days, before the biology that matters even begins. We built Yuna to close that gap.”

The company has backed up that claim with public data. A preprint posted to bioRxiv documents Yuna reproducing three known skin conditions across the full four-week window, sustained psoriasis-like inflammation that responded to a JAK inhibitor, senescence markers in aged donor tissue that dropped after a senolytic treatment and UV damage that a topical sunscreen measurably reduced. None of those outcomes, Outer Bio argues, would have shown up in a shorter-lived model.
A longevity tool wearing a skincare label

It’s easy to file this under beauty industry news and move on. However, the underlying idea (senescent cells accumulating, inflammation quietly compounding, tissue losing its ability to repair itself) is the same biology longevity researchers chase in every other organ in the body. Skin just happens to be the one organ scientists can study without surgery, which makes it a useful proving ground for aging science more broadly.

If a platform like Yuna can reliably show that a senolytic combination reverses senescence markers in living tissue, that’s a data point for aging research well beyond what shows up on a store shelf. Outer Bio is opening the platform to select biopharma and ingredient partners, meaning its four-week window may end up informing therapeutics as much as it does the next serum.

articles.titleKo: 아우터 바이오는 과학자들에게 노화 피부를 연구할 한 달을 제공합니다
articles.summaryKo: 아우터 바이오의 유나 플랫폼은 한 달 동안 살아있는 인간 피부가 기능하도록 유지하며, 이는 실제로 눈에 띄는 노화를 늦추는 요인을 테스트할 수 있는 더 긴 기간입니다. 몸에서 인간 피부 한 조각을 잘라내면 시간이 흐르기 시작합니다. 며칠 만에 피부처럼 전혀 행동하지 않습니다. 한때 염증과 싸우고 콜라겐을 재구성하며 [...] 아우터 바이오가 과학자들에게 노화 피부를 연구할 한 달을 제공했다는 글이 나왔습니다
bodyKo: 아우터 바이오의 유나 플랫폼은 한 달 동안 인간의 피부 기능을 유지하며, 이는 실제로 눈에 띄는 노화를 늦추는 요인을 테스트할 수 있는 더 긴 기간입니다.

몸에서 인간 피부 한 조각을 잘라내면 시간이 흐르기 시작합니다. 며칠 만에 피부처럼 전혀 행동하지 않습니다. 염증과 싸우고, 콜라겐을 재구성하며, 상처를 치유했던 세포들이 점차 기능을 멈추기 시작합니다. 어떤 화합물이 실제로 피부 노화를 늦추는지 알아내려는 과학자들에게 그 짧은 시간이 항상 문제였습니다. 검사 조직이 1주 차도 채 지나지 않고 죽었다면, 몇 주가 걸리는 과정을 지켜볼 수 없습니다.
새로운 회사는 그 수수께끼를 풀었다고 생각한다. Outer Bio는 이번 주에 Yuna라는 플랫폼을 은밀하게 출시했는데, 이 플랫폼은 인간의 피부(표피, 진피, 면역 세포 포함)를 4주 동안 살아 있고 검사 가능하게 유지한다 [1]. 회사는 이 정도면 노화 피부 뒤에 있는 느린 생물학적 과정을 실제 인간 조직에서 실시간으로 관찰하기에 충분하다고 말한다.
스킨케어는 1,000억 달러가 넘는 산업이지만, 30년에 걸친 연구 끝에 단 하나의 국소 성분(여기 레티노이드)만이 노화 피부를 눈에 띄게 개선한다는 이유로 FDA로부터 인정을 받았습니다.

아우터 바이오의 주장은 이것이 시도 부족이나 자금 부족 때문이 아니라는 것이다. 이것은 기술적인 병목 현상이다. 노화 피부에 중요한 생물학 – 콜라겐이 어떻게 재건되는지, 만성 저등급 염증('인플램징'이라고 롱제비티 연구자들이 부르는 표현)이 어떻게 손상을 일으키는지, 노쇠한 세포가 어떻게 쌓여 기능을 멈추는지는 몇 주가 걸린다. 표준 실험실 피부는 그렇게 오래 버틸 수 없기 때문에, 연구자들은 사실상 마라톤을 처음 100야드만 관찰하며 판단해야 한다.

Yuna는 이러한 제약을 없애도록 설계되었습니다. 조직은 다양한 연령, 성별, 피부색을 가진 기증자들로부터 나오며, 한 달 내내 지속적으로 추적됩니다. Cell 활성, 조직 구조, 단백질 신호. 각 검사 화합물은 30,000개 이상의 데이터 포인트를 생성하며, 회사는 이미 300명 이상의 기증자와 10,000건의 개별 치료에서 10테라바이트 이상의 데이터를 수집했다고 밝혔습니다.

이 생체 조직 데이터는 매 테스트마다 점점 더 똑똑해지는 머신러닝 시스템에 공급되도록 설계되었습니다. 유나의 결과를 기반으로 학습된 모델은 다음에 어떤 화합물을 우선순위를 정하고, 새로운 결과가 나올 때마다 예측이 더욱 날카로워집니다. 아우터 바이오는 가상 스크리닝 라이브러리가 이미 590만 개의 화합물을 커버하고 있으며, 앞으로 수십억 개의 라이브러리를 통해 연구할 계획이라고 밝혔습니다.

"스킨케어는 수요나 야망이 부족한 적이 없습니다. 생물학적으로 중요한 시간 동안 살아있는 인간 피부의 화합물과 메커니즘을 연구할 능력이 부족했습니다,"라고 아우터 바이오의 공동 창립자이자 CEO인 마이클 폴란스키가 말했습니다. "대부분의 실험 플랫폼은 재구성된 피부나 세포 단층에 의존합니다. 그 모델들은 화합물이 독성인지 알려줄 수 있지만; 실제 장기의 복잡성과 구조가 부족하기 때문에 효과가 있는지는 알 수 없습니다. 그리고 중요한 생물학이 시작되기 전 며칠 내에 실패합니다. 우리는 그 격차를 메우기 위해 유나를 만들었습니다."

이 회사는 공개 데이터로 이 주장을 뒷받침했다. bioRxiv에 게시된 프리프린트에는 유나가 4주 전체 기간 동안 세 가지 알려진 피부 질환을 재현한 내용이 기록되어 있다. JAK 억제제에 반응한 지속적인 건선 유사 염증, 세놀리틱 치료 후 노화된 기증자 조직의 노화세포 마커, 그리고 국소 자외선 차단제로 측정 가능한 자외선 손상을 측정한 결과이다. 아우터 바이오는 이러한 결과들 중 어느 것도 단수명 모델에서는 나타나지 않았을 것이라고 주장한다.
스킨케어 라벨을 붙인 롱제비티 도구
이것을 미용 산업 뉴스로 분류하고 넘어가기 쉽습니다. 하지만 근본적인 개념(노화 세포 축적, 염증 조용히 복합, 조직 스스로 회복 능력 상실)은 롱제비티 연구자들이 신체의 다른 모든 장기에서 쫓는 동일한 생물학적 원리입니다. 피부는 과학자들이 수술 없이도 연구할 수 있는 유일한 장기로, 노화 과학 전반에 유용한 시험장이 됩니다.

Yuna와 같은 플랫폼이 세놀리틱 조합이 살아있는 조직의 노화세포 마커를 되돌린다는 것을 신뢰성 있게 입증한다면, 이는 노화 연구에 있어 매장 진열대에 나오는 것보다 훨씬 더 큰 데이터 포인트가 될 것입니다. Outer Bio는 바이오제약 및 성분 파트너를 선정하여 플랫폼을 개방하고 있어, 4주 기간이 다음 세럼만큼이나 치료제에도 영향을 미칠 수 있습니다.
[1] https://www.outerbio.com/news/outer-bio-emerges-from-stealth-with-yuna-a-platform-that-keeps-ex-vivo-human-skin-alive-and-measurable-for-four-weeks
"아우터 바이오가 과학자들에게 노화 피부를 연구할 한 달 시간을 제공한다"는 글이 롱제비티에 처음 게재되었습니다. 기술.

bodyOriginal.text: Sam Altman-backed Retro Biosciences is widening its Alzheimer’s trial after early doses showed no red flags .
Most drug trials pray for a boring readout. Retro Biosciences got exactly that, and now it has a problem precisely because nothing went wrong.

The Sam Altman-funded longevity startup is testing a pill called RTR-242, designed to help the brain clear out cellular junk that piles up with age and is thought to worsen conditions like Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s [ 1 ].

According to Retro CEO Joe Betts-LaCroix, the drug’s early safety data has been almost suspiciously clean: no major side effects, no safety signals, nothing. Betts-LaCroix told Business Insider that’s a mixed blessing. Without any signal at all, it’s hard to know whether the drug is actually doing anything, or simply not doing enough.

So Retro is upping the dose and the headcount. The company is adding two new cohorts to its Phase 1 safety trial, expanding total enrollment by more than 42%, from 76 to 108 participants. The hope, somewhat counterintuitively, is to see something.
“Hopefully, at some point, we will at least get headaches or something,” Betts-LaCroix said, only half-joking about the search for a dose potent enough to matter without becoming unsafe.
Joe Betts-LaCroix is founder and CEO of Retro Biosciences.

RTR-242 targets lysosomes, the recycling centers inside every cell that break down old, damaged proteins so the cell can reuse the parts. That recycling process, called autophagy, tends to slow down with age, and researchers increasingly view a sluggish cleanup system as one of the threads connecting general aging to specific neurodegenerative diseases. Retro’s drug is designed to restore the acidity that aging lysosomes lose, essentially sharpening a dulled tool rather than replacing it.

Retro isn’t alone in betting on this mechanism. Boston-based Lysoway Therapeutics began its own first-in-human trial targeting lysosomes in May, backed in part by the Michael J Fox Foundation. That same month, Chicago’s Vanqua Bio reported promising early safety results from a similar approach aimed at Parkinson’s. It’s a crowded corner of neuroscience, but crowded doesn’t mean solved; nobody has yet proven a lysosome-targeting drug works in patients.

Paul Robbins, a biochemist and longevity researcher at the University of Minnesota who isn’t involved in the Retro trial, called the lysosome an “interesting target,” particularly for cognitive decline. He said he’s encouraged by the lack of toxicity so far, but wants to see more before celebrating.

“If they’re not seeing toxicity, that’s great,” Robbins said, adding that he doesn’t yet know exactly how the drug works or whether it will help people who actually have dementia, since RTR-242 is currently being tested only in healthy volunteers ages 18 to 65.
For Betts-LaCroix, the project isn’t abstract. He lost his father to Alzheimer’s earlier this year.
“You make it into your 90s and then, damn. It comes along and strips your personhood out right from under you,” he said.

That’s really the pitch behind the whole longevity category Retro competes in: not immortality, but more good years, and fewer of them lost to diseases that erase who a person is before the body gives out.

Retro Biosciences says its broader mission is adding ten healthy years to the human lifespan, and RTR-242 is its most concrete swing at that goal so far. Rivals like Altos Labs and New Limit are working on their own approaches to aging biology, but as of now, neither has announced a drug in human trials, which puts Retro, for the moment, a step ahead in the race to find the first genuine longevity drug. Whether that lead holds may come down to something as unglamorous as finding the right dose.

articles.titleKo: 레트로 바이오사이언스가 알츠하이머 약 용량을 조정하다
articles.summaryKo: 샘 알트만이 지원하는 레트로 바이오사이언스는 초기 투여에서 아무런 경고 신호가 없어 알츠하이머 임상시험을 확대하고 있다. 대부분의 약물 임상시험은 지루한 결과만 나오길 바란다. 레트로 바이오사이언스는 바로 그런 결과를 얻었고, 아무 문제도 없었기 때문에 이제 문제가 생겼다. 샘 알트만이 자금을 지원하는 롱제비티 스타트업은 RTR-242라는 알약을 시험하고 있으며, 이는 [...] 레트로 바이오사이언스가 알츠하이머를 약간 조정하다
bodyKo: 샘 알트만이 지원하는 레트로 바이오사이언스는 초기 접종 결과에 이상 징후가 없어 알츠하이머 임상시험을 확대하고 있습니다.
대부분의 신약 임상시험은 지루한 결과만 나오길 바란다. 레트로 바이오사이언스는 바로 그 결과를 얻었고, 아무 문제도 없었기 때문에 문제가 생겼다.
샘 알트만이 자금을 지원하는 롱제비티 스타트업은 RTR-242라는 알약을 시험 중인데, 이 약은 나이가 들면서 쌓이는 세포 정체를 제거하도록 돕기 위해 고안되었으며, 알츠하이머병과 파킨슨병 같은 질환을 악화시키는 것으로 여겨집니다 [1].

Retro CEO 조 베츠-라크루아에 따르면, 이 약물의 초기 안전성 데이터는 거의 의심스러울 정도로 깨끗했습니다: 주요 부작용도 없고, 안전 신호도 없으며, 아무것도 없습니다. 베츠-라크루아는 비즈니스 인사이더와의 인터뷰에서 이것이 복합된 축복이라고 말했습니다. 전혀 신호가 없으면 약물이 실제로 효과가 있는지, 아니면 단순히 충분히 효과가 없는지 알기 어렵습니다.
그래서 레트로는 용량과 인원을 늘리고 있습니다. 회사는 1상 안전성 시험에 두 명의 새로운 코호트를 추가하여 총 등록 인원을 76명에서 108명으로 42% 이상 늘렸습니다. 다소 직관에 반하는 희망은 무언가를 보는 것입니다.
"언젠가는 적어도 두통이나 그런 일이 생길 거야," 베츠-라크루아가 말했다. 위험하지 않으면서도 의미 있을 만큼 강력한 용량을 찾는 과정에 대해 반쯤 농담 섞인 듯했다.
조 베츠-라크루아는 Retro Biosciences의 창립자이자 CEO입니다.

RTR-242는 모든 세포 내부의 재활용 센터인 라이소좀을 표적으로 삼는데, 이 센터는 오래되고 손상된 단백질을 분해해 세포가 그 부품을 재사용할 수 있게 합니다. 이 재활용 과정인 자가포식은 나이가 들수록 느려지는 경향이 있으며, 연구자들은 점점 느린 정화 시스템을 일반적인 노화와 특정 신경퇴행성 질환을 연결하는 실마리 중 하나로 보고 있습니다. 레트로의 약물은 노화 리소좀이 잃는 산도를 회복하도록 설계되어, 본질적으로 무뎌진 도구를 교체하는 것이 아니라 연마시키는 것입니다.

레트로만 이 메커니즘에 베팅하는 것은 아닙니다. 보스턴에 본사를 둔 라이소웨이 테라퓨틱스는 마이클 J 폭스 재단의 일부 지원을 받아 5월에 라이소좀을 대상으로 한 최초의 인간 대상 임상시험을 시작했습니다. 같은 달, 시카고의 반콰 바이오는 파킨슨병을 겨냥한 유사한 접근법에서 유망한 초기 안전성 결과를 보고했습니다. 신경과학 분야에서 경쟁이 치열한 분야이지만, 혼잡하다고 해서 해결된 것은 아닙니다; 아직 아무도 환자에게 리소좀 표적 약물이 효과가 있음을 증명하지 않았습니다.
미네소타 대학교의 생화학자이자 롱제비티 연구자인 폴 로빈스는 리소좀을 특히 인지 저하에 있어 "흥미로운 표적"이라고 평가했습니다. 그는 지금까지 독성이 없다는 점에 고무적이지만, 축하하기 전에 더 많은 결과를 보고 싶다고 말했습니다.
"독성이 없다면 다행입니다,"라고 로빈스는 말하며, 현재 RTR-242가 18세에서 65세 사이의 건강한 자원자에게만 시험되고 있어 약물이 정확히 어떻게 작용하는지, 실제 치매 환자에게 도움이 될지 아직 알지 못한다고 덧붙였습니다.
베츠-라크루아에게 이 프로젝트는 추상적이지 않습니다. 그는 올해 초 알츠하이머로 아버지를 잃었습니다.
"90대가 되어서, 젠장. 그게 와서 네 인격을 완전히 빼앗아가게 해," 그가 말했다.
이것이 바로 레트로가 경쟁하는 롱제비티 장수 카테고리의 핵심입니다: 불멸이 아니라, 더 많은 좋은 해를 보내고, 몸이 고장 나기 전에 사람을 지워버리는 질병으로 잃는 시간이 적다는 것입니다.

레트로 바이오사이언스는 인간의 건강한 수명을 10년을 늘리는 것이 더 넓은 목표라고 밝혔으며, RTR-242는 지금까지 그 목표에 가장 구체적인 변화입니다. Altos Labs와 New Limit 같은 경쟁사들은 노화 생물학에 대한 독자적인 접근법을 개발 중이지만, 현재까지 두 곳 모두 인간 임상시험에서 약물을 발표하지 않아 레트로가 최초의 진정한 롱제비티 약물을 찾는 경쟁에서 한 발 앞서 나가고 있음을 의미합니다. 그 선두가 유지될지는 적절한 용량을 찾는 것과 같은 화려하지 않은 문제일 수 있습니다.
[1] https://www.businessinsider.com/retro-biotech-testing-higher-doses-of-rtr-242-alzheimers-drug-2026-8
레트로 바이오사이언스가 알츠하이머 알츠하이머 약 용량을 조정하다 보도, 이 글은 롱제비티에 처음 게재되었습니다. 기술.

articles.titleOriginal: Apple Watch can now estimate your ‘health age’
articles.summaryOriginal: New sensors, a daily readiness score and a Health Age feature aim to make longevity insight as routine as checking the time. Most people check their Apple Watch for the time, a text, maybe how many steps they’ve logged. Soon, quite a few of them will glance down and see something closer to a verdict […] The post Apple Watch can now estimate your ‘health age’ appeared first on Longevity.Technology

bodyOriginal.text: New sensors, a daily readiness score and a Health Age feature aim to make longevity insight as routine as checking the time.

Most people check their Apple Watch for the time, a text, maybe how many steps they’ve logged. Soon, quite a few of them will glance down and see something closer to a verdict on how well their body is actually holding up. Apple announced its biggest health and fitness overhaul in years on 9 September, and tucked inside the usual product-launch language is a genuinely new idea for a mainstream device: a number meant to reflect how old your body behaves, not just how many birthdays it’s had [ 1 ].

The hardware side is Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4, both built around a reworked Health Sensing System. The software side, a rebuilt Health app, arrives on iPhone later this year and leans on Apple Intelligence to turn a mess of biometric data into something a non-scientist can read.

Start with the sensors, because that’s genuinely where things changed. Apple swapped in larger, more efficient green LEDs on the optical heart sensor, which lets the watch measure heart rate every five seconds, continuously, all day. Older models sampled far less often. Heart rate variability (HRV, the metric researchers lean on as a stress and recovery signal) now refreshes roughly every five minutes, a 24-fold jump in frequency compared with before.

Apple also split HRV into two separate readings instead of one catch-all number. Recovery HRV tracks short-term stress, the kind that spikes after a bad night’s sleep or a brutal training session. Overall HRV moves more slowly and speaks to broader cardiovascular health. Higher variability, generally, tracks with a body that’s coping better.

None of that data means much sitting on its own, though. Apple’s answer is a new daily readiness score, rated 0 to 10, built from recent activity, vitals and sleep, paired with a plain-language nudge: recover, pace yourself, ready or go for it. Whether that lands as helpful or as one more thing nagging at you probably depends on the person.

Apple says the accuracy behind all this isn’t just a claim. The company ran a study with more than 1,000 participants across a range of demographic groups, comparing its new heart sensing against several leading wearables already on shelves, and reports Apple Watch came out ahead on accuracy across the group.

For readers who follow longevity science closely, the part worth lingering on sits inside the Health app: a new Longevity tab. It folds heart health, sleep, mental wellbeing, movement, metabolic health, hearing and nutrition into a single longitudinal view instead of scattering them across separate screens, which is how the app has worked for most of its life. Its centerpiece, Health Age, estimates how someone’s metrics are tracking against their actual age, drawing on VO2 max, resting heart rate, sleep quality and HRV. Users can layer in lab results, too, including A1c and LDL cholesterol, to sharpen the estimate.
It’s a simplified, wrist-based cousin of the biological age clocks that longevity researchers have been refining in labs for years, only now it’s sitting next to your text messages.

“At Apple, we believe technology can empower everyone with actionable, science-based insights built with privacy at the core,” said Dr Sumbul Desai, Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness. “By combining breakthrough sensing on Apple Watch with Apple Intelligence in the Health app, we’re able to translate complex biometric data into clear guidance for users. This both helps people navigate their day-to-day routines with confidence and connects those moments with deeper context around their longevity, building a strong foundation for a healthier future.”
Phil Newman, Editor-in-Chief: The charging friction in Apple’s longevity push

Having spent years in product development, I have sat in my share of scoping sessions where engineers and marketers convince themselves that users will happily adjust their daily habits for a clever new feature. Post-launch, reality usually has the final say.

I love my Apple Watch, but it goes straight onto the charger when I head to bed and doesn’t cross my mind again until morning. Instead, I rely on my 24-hour Whoop to track overnight recovery and plan my daily training. That highlights the immediate practical wall Apple’s new ‘Health Age’ metric and Longevity tab hit: battery life. Over-the-air recovery metrics rely heavily on overnight sleep data, yet the vast majority of owners take off their devices to charge while sleeping.

Unless users adopt clunky workaround routines – like topping off battery levels twice daily or buying specialized third-party power banks – Apple’s recovery algorithms won’t get the data they need to be truly meaningful.

The real inflection point will arrive if rumors of Apple developing a screenless, continuous-wear device prove true. That is when Apple’s longevity proposition will really start to bite into ŌURA and Whoop revenues – and perhaps drive a valuation rethink for investors when ŌURA goes public. Until then, as long as Whoop’s IP team holds their ground on wrist-worn battery patents, pure-play wearables retain a distinct operational edge, even as Apple brings longevity into the mainstream consumer lexicon.

There’s also a mobility piece easy to miss in the announcement but relevant to anyone in longevity medicine. Most people never get formally assessed for flexibility, balance or movement mechanics unless something has already gone wrong, since that usually means booking time with a physical therapist.

The new Health app lets users run those assessments at home using an iPhone camera and Apple Watch, with on-device, vision-based AI models built alongside clinicians; no video is ever recorded or stored, a detail that will matter to anyone wary of camera-based health tools.

Lab testing is now bookable through roughly 2,000 Quest Diagnostics locations in the US, covering more than 50 biomarkers for $119. Cycle Tracking has also been expanded to flag perimenopause and menopause, an area of women’s health that’s historically gotten far less attention from consumer tech than it deserves.

None of this treats or diagnoses anything, and Apple says as much; the Vitals app, by its own description, is for wellness use, not medical use. But it’s worth noticing the direction a device worn by hundreds of millions of people is heading. Healthspan, not just lifespan, is exactly the framing longevity researchers have been pushing for years, and now it’s showing up on ordinary wrists rather than in academic papers.

Whether Health Age turns into something people actually act on, or just becomes a fancier step counter, is still an open question. It starts rolling out with watchOS 27 on 14 September, so we’ll find out soon enough.
